commit.message:
Extend the test to run on Linux, macOS, and on Windows

- To maintain compatibility with `handle_stack_overflow()` in
  os_posix.cpp, the handler for `EXCEPTION_STACK_OVERFLOW` does not
  check for `_thread_in_vm` or `_thread_in_native`.  All non-Java
  executions continue execution.

- TestWindowsStackOverflow (renamed to TestStackOverflowExceptions) is
  now a cross-platform test (it runs on Linux, Windows, and macOS).

- That test checks the following scenarios:

   - Unrecoverable overflow handling (after touching a red zone page)

   - Recoverable overflow handling from _Java_ threads (interpreter, C1,
     and C2)

   - Recoverable overflow handling from _native_ threads (interpreter,
     C1, and C2)

   - Back-to-back recoverable overflow handling (to exercise both code
     paths on Windows)

- Since this patch no longer restricts `StackLimit` growth to just
  Java-thread execution (since a native thread, too, could potentially
  bang past `StackLimit`), I've updated TestWindowsStackLimit to
  exercise both Java- and native-thread execution.

Use `PAGE_NOACCESS` instead of `PAGE_GUARD` for Yellow and Red zones

Prior to this patch, HotSpot on Windows used `PAGE_GUARD` protection
(which creates so-called Guard Pages) for Yellow and Red pages, but
guard pages provide a one-shot alarm that is handled by the OS and not
by HotSpot's signal handler, so HotSpot doesn't have control over how
Yellow and Red page accesses are handled.  Still, stack overflow
handling works, although by coincidence and not under all conditions,
since HotSpot's Yellow zone boundary happens to match Windows' default
terminal stack growth page.  The end result is that changing HotSpot's
Yellow or Red page count doesn't have the intended effect on stack
handling.

As a specific example, when Windows delivers `EXCEPTION_STACK_OVERFLOW`
to HotSpot, both Yellow and Red pages end up being writeable, so the Red
zone protection is effectively nullified.  Continued stack usage
eventually terminates the JVM, but that's because those accesses land in
the so-called bottom page (which again, just happens to match the lone
Red page in HotSpot).  Unless specified, Windows marks this bottom page
as non-readable and non-writeable, whereas in HotSpot, we may need to
use the Red zone pages, so HotSpot cannot rely on default Windows
behavior.  Put another way, if the Windows' defaults were to change,
HotSpot's stack overflow handling will break.

This patch brings stack overflow handling under HotSpot's control,
primarily by switching to `PAGE_NOACCESS` protection for Yellow and Red
pages.  HotSpot now responds to the `EXCEPTION_STACK_OVERFLOW` exception
(triggered by Windows running out of stack pages to commit) and to the
`EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION` exception (triggered by accesses to Red and
Yellow pages).  This patch includes some ancillary fixes, like detecting
nested stack overflow exceptions and unexpected thread states, in
addition to overall simplification of the code.

In the interest of limiting the diff size, this patch does not address
the coincidence that HotSpot's existing Yellow pages align with Windows'
terminal growth page.  Fixing that requires dynamically inflating
HotSpot's Yellow zone size depending on Windows' terminal growth page,
which is a function of the thread stack guarantee.  A subsequent patch
will query and set the Windows thread stack guarantee at run-time to
adjust the yellow zone size.

I validated this patch by running through tier 1 through 3 tests in the
JDK, HotSpot, and LangTools test groups on both Windows/x64 and
Windows/ARM64.
